one_liner: Drop-in malloc that compacts fragmented C/C++ heaps by page remapping; 16% less memory than Firefox's jemalloc, 39% on Redis.
what_it_does: Mesh is a malloc(3) replacement (libmesh.so, used via LD_PRELOAD or linking) that returns physical memory lost to fragmentation without moving pointers or changing application code. It exports the standard malloc/free/realloc/calloc/memalign family plus mallctl-style tuning, and prints meshing statistics at exit when MALLOCSTATS=1.
how_it_is_fast: Meshing: when two spans of the same size class have non-overlapping live objects, Mesh copies one span's objects into the other's physical page and remaps both virtual spans onto that one physical span (the arena is a memfd_create-backed shared mapping, so mmap can alias offsets), so object addresses never change. Candidate pairs come from SplitMesher, a randomized matching algorithm with a probabilistic guarantee, and shuffle vectors randomize object placement within spans at bump-pointer cost so pages stay meshable. Meshing runs concurrently, using mprotect plus a SIGSEGV handler as a write barrier, and is rate-limited (default at most every 100 ms).
when_to_use: Long-running, allocation-heavy servers or browsers whose RSS grows from fragmentation (many small objects of mixed lifetimes), e.g. Redis-style caches where you would otherwise rely on jemalloc's active defragmentation.
You cannot change the application (no custom arenas, no defrag API) but can LD_PRELOAD an allocator on Linux or macOS.
Memory-constrained deployments where a few percent runtime overhead is acceptable for 15-40% lower heap size on fragmenting workloads.
Workloads with regular allocate/free patterns (the paper's Ruby microbenchmark), where randomized placement gives meshing room that non-randomized allocators lack.
when_not_to_use: You want speed: Mesh does not beat glibc or jemalloc on runtime; the paper shows +0.7% SPECint geomean, +3.9% on perlbench and +10.7% on the Ruby microbenchmark, and Redis insertion took 1.76 s vs 1.72 s with jemalloc.
Workloads without fragmentation or dominated by objects over 16 KiB: large objects bypass meshing, and SPECint memory only dropped 2.4% geomean.

Programs that install their own SIGSEGV handlers or rely on fault handling (JVMs, sanitizers, some runtimes): Mesh interposes sigaction for its write barrier, and open issues report segfaults under OpenJDK 16 (#87) and when preloaded (#72, #99).

Applications that depend on transparent huge pages: meshing works at 4 KiB (16 KiB on Apple Silicon) granularity and the paper notes poor interaction with THP; huge-page support is an open issue (#89).
Some users report higher memory than jemalloc 5.1, Chrome or Firefox (#116, #45, #67), and there are no tagged releases (#114).

integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond libc; build uses Bazel wrapped in a Makefile (CMakeLists.txt also present, fetching Heap Layers and googletest)
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS on x86-64; aarch64 build flags and Apple Silicon 16 KiB pages handled in recent code; Windows work in progress; 32-bit unsupported
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe: per-thread heaps with shuffle vectors, atomic bitmaps for remote frees, global heap lock held during meshing; fork/spawn races fixed in January 2026

gotchas: Reserves a 64 GB virtual arena on Linux (32 GB on macOS) backed by a memfd temporary file, so strict overcommit or address-space limits can break it.
Meshing adds page-table entries and brief pauses (paper: max 7.5 ms on Firefox, 22 ms on Redis); tune with MESH_PERIOD_MS, MESH_BACKGROUND_THREAD or mallctl.
The CMake RANDOMIZATION option (0, 1 or 2) and DISABLE_MESHING change behavior; with randomization off the Ruby benchmark saved only 3%.
Memory must be measured as RSS including page tables (the paper used its mstat cgroup tool); allocator-reported heap sizes do not show meshing savings.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Mesh over speed-oriented siblings such as v8malloc, FastAlloc or Spaces when fragmentation-driven RSS is the problem and you accept equal-or-slightly-slower runtime; IsoAlloc targets hardening, and libpas returns pages sooner but only inside WebKit, while Mesh is the only catalogued allocator that compacts an unmodified C/C++ heap.
verified_claims_summary: The PLDI 2019 paper ran on an Intel i7-5600U with 16 GiB under Linux 4.18 (SPEC built with clang 4.0 -O2, Mesh with gcc 8 -O3 -flto): mean RSS on Firefox 57 Speedometer was 530 MB vs 632 MB with bundled jemalloc (16%, under 1% score loss); Redis 4.0.2 got the same 39% heap reduction as jemalloc 3.6.0 active defrag with 0.23 s of meshing vs 1.49 s of defrag; 400.perlbench peak RSS was 564 MB vs 664 MB glibc 2.26 (+3.9% runtime); SPECint geomean -2.4% memory, +0.7% time.
status_note: Active again (commits through 2026-03-25 fixing fork races, signal handling, aarch64 atomics), Apache-2.0, 1.9k stars, but 29 open issues including crashes and build failures on several distros and no releases.
